newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda studies bid for 51 percent of coffee board.
newsitem.headline: Uganda studies bid for 51 percent of coffee board.

text.p: The Ugandan government, pushing ahead with an ambitious privatisation programme, said on Wednesday it was evaluating a bid for 51 percent of its shares in the key Coffee Marketing Board (CMBL).
Anne Bwomezi, spokesperson for the government's privatisation unit, told Reuters only one company, Swiss coffee house Sucafina, had bid for CMBL, currently 100-percent controlled by the government.
"There was only bid and it is now being evaluated. A committee will decide whether it is worth it or the company should be readvertised," she told Reuters in Kampala.
Bwomezi declined to say when the final decision would be made.

Officials said Sucafina had offered to pay $3.3 million for CMBL's processing plant in Kampala and buying centres countrywide. The plant has the capacity to process up to four million 60-kg bags of coffee and handles half the country's coffee exports.
No comment was immediately available from Geneva-based Sucafina.
CMBL, which also markets coffee, is currently valued at about $36 million, senior privatisation officials said.
The government would retain a 49 percent shareholding and was separately selling off non-core assets such as CMBL's office blocks abroad, residential houses and heavy-duty vehicles.
If successful, the buying company would assume the liabilities of the coffee plant, Bwomezi said. She did not have figures on these.

But other officials said that in considering Sucafina's bid, the Ugandan government would consider the possible benefits of a more efficient operation that would generate profits and increase the worth of the government's shares.
"We shall be taking into account the possible profits to be generated after the company has been divested," an official close to the evaluation process told Reuters.
The sale of CMBL is part of a wider privatisation programme encouraged by Western donors.

Most companies are being sold off completely, but the government recently announced it would retain shares in those likely to be profitable, simply handing over their management to others so as to raise the worth of their shareholding before a final sell-off.
Officials in the finance ministry said full divestiture of the coffee board would take place as soon as a planned stock exchange takes off, probably in October or November.
The sale of CMBL would be the final step towards liberalising Uganda's coffee industry, which fetches up to 70 percent of its hard currency earnings.
Uganda introduced reforms in the industry in 1991, licensing private buyers, who now sell beans direct on the world market.
